header.author: Cassiodorus Vivariensis Abbas
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's tmp1179.tmp1179.opp-lat1, from Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. notes.urn:cts:latinLit:tmp1179.tmp1179.opp-lat: The printed text has many OCR errors (e.g. 'honestum. que' for honestumque, 'eam' and 'cum' for eum, 'videtut', 'pervenfte', 'qnod') and stray footnote letters and a page number (57), which are not translated. The bracketed variant readings, '[Jur. forte pravitate]' and '(Vide Cypr. lib. de Spectac.)' are the editor's, translated in brackets and parentheses. 'Elis, a city of Asia' is as the text has it. 'He at once took up a faction ... that was failing' (protinus inclinatam) may instead mean a faction that at once inclined to him. 'Where an image of a head is known to be at work' (imago capiti[s]) is obscure. 'Mothers of birds' (avium matribus) is unclear in sense.

Footnote signs and OCR errors in the printed text are not translated. '(See Baronius, at the year of Christ 504)' is the editor's insertion, not Cassiodorus. 'The punishable muttering of souls' (poenale murmur animarum) presumably refers to incantations addressed to the dead; the sense is not certain.

nodes.text: As rare as steadfastness and an honourable aim are among performers, so much the more precious is a commendable disposition when it is shown in them. For it is a dear thing to a man to have found something praiseworthy where he had not thought to find it. Some time ago, indeed, our consideration granted reasonable allowances to Thomas the charioteer, who came to us from the regions of the East, until we should test his skill and his spirit. But since he is known to hold first place in this contest, and his will, his homeland left behind, has chosen to cherish the seat of our rule, we have decided that he should be secured with a monthly bounty, so as not to leave still uncertain one whom we know to have chosen the dominion of Italy. For he, often a victor, has flown through the mouths of many, carried more by favour than by chariots. He at once took up a faction of the people that was failing, and those whom he himself had made sad he laboured to make glad again, now surpassing the drivers by skill, now outstripping them by the speed of his horses. The frequency of his palms caused him to be called a sorcerer, and among them it seems a great distinction to arrive at such charges. For victory must be put down to magical perversity when it cannot be credited to the merits of the horses. [It is] a spectacle that drives out the most serious morals and invites the most frivolous quarrels, an emptying of decency, a well-watered spring of brawls, which antiquity indeed held sacred, but quarrelsome posterity has made a mockery [another reading: a slippery thing]. For Oenomaus is said to have first put it on at Elis, a city of Asia; afterwards Romulus, at the seizure of the Sabine women, before any buildings had been founded, displayed it to Italy in rustic fashion. But Augustus, lord of the world, raising the work to match his power, stretched a structure wondrous even to Romans across the Murcian valley, so that an immense mass, firmly girt by hills, should enclose [a place] where tokens of great things were shut in. For they set twelve gates for the twelve signs. These are opened with sudden evenness by ropes let down from little herms, showing that everything there, as was thought, is done by design, where an image of a head is known to be at work. The colours, moreover, are laid out in a fourfold division after the seasons: green is dedicated to verdant spring, blue to cloudy winter, red to flaming summer, white to frosty autumn, so that the whole year, as if passing through the twelve signs, should be signified. So it came about that the workings of nature were played out in the contrived imagery of the spectacles. The two-horse chariot was devised as if in imitation of the moon, the four-horse chariot of the sun. The horses of the vaulting riders, by which the attendants of the circus announce that the heats are about to go out, imitate the forerunning speed of the morning star. So it happened that, while they thought they were worshipping the stars, they profaned their religion with a playful likeness. A white line is drawn, not far from the gates, to each podium, straight as if by a ruler, so that the contest should start from there as the four-horse chariots advance, lest, while they always strive in haste to dash one another out, they should seem to rob the people of the pleasure of watching. The whole contest is completed in seven rounds of the turning-posts, in the likeness of the recurring week. The turning-posts themselves have three peaks each, after the decans of the zodiac, and the swift four-horse chariots range around them like the sun. The wheels mark the bounds of East and West. The Euripus gives back the image of the glassy sea, whence sea dolphins swim through the waters there. The tall shafts of the obelisks too are raised to the height of heaven; but the greater is dedicated to the sun, the lesser to the moon; on them the rites of the ancients are indicated by Chaldaean signs, as if by letters. The *spina* [the central barrier] signifies the lot of unhappy captives, where the generals of the Romans, walking over the backs of their enemies, received the joys of their labours. The napkin, which is seen to give the signal for the circus games, passed into custom by this chance: when Nero was prolonging his lunch, and the people, eager to watch, were demanding haste as usual, he ordered the napkin he was using to wipe his hands to be thrown out of the window, to give leave for the contest demanded [some read 'to be demanded'; others 'to the one demanding']. From this it has come about that the showing of the napkin seems a sure promise of circus games to come. The circus is named from 'going round' (*circuitus*); *circenses* as if *circuenses*, because in rude antiquity, which had not yet brought spectacles into the adornment of buildings, they were held between swords (*enses*) and rivers in green places. Nor is it without meaning that the terms of this contest are fulfilled in twenty-four heats, so that the hours of day and night should be comprised in that number. Nor let it be thought idle that the circuit of the turning-posts is marked by the raising of eggs, since the performance itself, pregnant with many superstitions, professes by the example of the egg that it will give birth to something. And so we are given to understand that flighty and most inconstant ways are born from it, which they have fitted to the mothers of birds. It would be long to run through the rest of the Roman circus in words, since all of it seems to relate to particular causes. This only we say is in every way astonishing: that there, beyond other spectacles, the fervour of minds is swept away with thoughtless gravity [Jur.: perhaps 'depravity'] (See Cyprian, book On Spectacles). The Green passes, a part of the people grieves; the Blue takes the lead, and the greater crowd of the city is afflicted; gaining nothing, they jeer hotly; suffering nothing, they are gravely wounded; and they descend to empty quarrels as if they were struggling for the state of an imperilled fatherland. This is rightly believed to be dedicated to manifold superstition, since it is plain that there one falls so far from decent ways. We foster these things out of necessity, because of the people pressing upon us, whose wish it is to gather for such things while they delight to cast away serious thoughts. For reason captures few, and a worthy purpose delights rare men, and the crowd is drawn rather to what is known to have been devised for the relief of cares. For whatever it reckons pleasurable, it judges this too should be counted toward the happiness of the times. Therefore let us bestow the expenses; let us not always give according to judgement. It is sometimes expedient to play the fool, so that we can keep in hand the joys the people long for.

An intolerable excess it is which aims at injury to the heavenly majesty and, forgetful of piety, pursues the cruelties of error. For what room for pardon has he hoped for, who has despised the Author who must be revered? Let the rite, now profane, depart from our midst; let the punishable muttering of souls fall silent. It is not permitted to be engaged in magic arts in Christian times (See Baronius, at the year of Christ 504). We have learned, then, from the report of Your Magnitude, that Basilius and Praetextatus, long polluted by the contagion of the sinister art, have been brought to accusation before your tribunal by the charge of [certain] persons. On this matter you declare that you await our decision, so that what the authority of Our Piety commands may be done with greater confidence. But we, who do not know how to depart from the laws, and whose concern it is to hold to a measured justice in all things, decree by the present authority that, with five senators, that is, the magnificent and patrician men Symmachus, Decius, Volusianus and Caelianus, and also the illustrious man Maximianus, you weigh this case by lawful examination. And if, with the order of law kept in every respect, the crime that is charged is proved, let it be punished with the full rigour of the laws themselves, so that hidden and secret offenders, whom uncertain knowledge cannot bring before the laws, may be kept from such crimes by this kind of punishment. On this matter we have sent instructions to the illustrious man Count Arigern, that, once every violent protection by anyone has been removed, he should drag the accused to judgement if they hide themselves, and, sitting with you in this case, should neither let the innocent be crushed nor allow the guilty to escape the laws.
